title: How can you establish that a character is a scientific genius without being hackneyed?

commenti.body:
This is an odd one but I think Silence of the Lambs does a good job of letting the audience know Hannibal Lecter is extremely competent and smart in a non overbearing way. 

The FBI is seeking his "expertise", he menacingly taunts Clarice with his understanding of the case that she wants to grasp, he outwits with clever escape attempts, he has respected credentials, etc.

None of his expertise is actionable.  He does not tell Clarice the unsub's name, location, etc., does not describe his appearance, etc.  Indeed, he tells her something she and every FBI agent already knows, e.g. that the unsub knew the first victim he killed, and thus she should canvass the victim's neighborhood.  I consider that an odd kind of expertise.  (What it really is is a demonstration of the FBI's inexpertise.)  Further, when Clarice goes to canvass the neighborhood, she goes alone.  That insures that she can go womano a mano with the unsub, but it also violates standard practice of the FBI and most police departments, real or fictional (e.g. Adam-12, Starsky and Hutch, Law & Order, Law & Order Criminal Intent, Law & Order Elevator Unit, and so on).  Oh yes Hannibal is clever; it astonishes me how unclever the FBI in that movie is.

So, yes, one can establish a character is a genius by contrasting him with idiots and incompetents.  Yes, movies and TV shows do this all the time.  It is all the more amazing in e.g. "The Cow Thief" (1962) episode of the Andy Griffith Show when Sheriff Taylor finds a cow thief when modern police methods can't.

>Recently I thought Oppenheimer did an okay job at this, but I think it was easier in that case because he was a smart man in rooms full of smart people, rather than a singular mind leaving everyone else in the dust.

It did fall back on clichés in regards to knowing language (I read it in the original German).
Ya, there’s definitely a reason I said okay and not great. I was still very impressed there wasn’t more of this because Nolan is just that kind of writer
To be fair that’s what the actual man was like. American Prometheus talks quite a bit about his love knowledge of other languages. The famous Dutch lecture and reading the Baghavad Gita in Sanskrit.
Fair enough. I quite liked the movie, but that moment was a little bad (especially since people have pointed out that the line isn't even accurate)

Arrival shows Dr. Louise Banks to be rather clever. They put her at odds with Renner’s character who’s a scientist and the general. But she wins her over with her methods. The story does a good job showing her reasoning and the systematic way she goes about understanding the aliens. The Kangaroo scene in particular communicates that well.

Yes. But if Oppenheimer had read Marx in the original German, he would have known that Marx did not say "property is theft" or anything similar in any language. So having Oppenheimer say he read it in the original German serves no purpose but to make him seem smart. It's a cliché, but that can be fine.
Fair enough I didn’t recall that specific scene.
[removed]

Completely agree. It also expertly circumnavigates the problem of having to explain (relatively) complex concepts within a film to the audience. Often my biggest gripe in these types of films is when scientists explain things to each other that they would all already know. Nolan is bad for this.

Not is she explaining things to other people who aren’t linguists, she’s explaining things that they couldn’t possible know because it’s a freakin’ alien language how could they.

I thought they handled it pretty well with Jodi Foster's Ellie Arroway in Contact. She was made to be an outsider simply for her SETI career choice, with multiple characters considering it to be a waste of limited telescope time. It's only when John Hurt's S.R. Hadden provides a biographical exposition about halfway through the film that we discover that Ellie is HIGHLY accomplished, in the potential-Nobel-prize category of scientists. However, she had zero interest in using her established profile for personal career gain, remaining pure in her pursuit of her scientific passions and belief in basic research regardless of any encountered political/realist hurdles.

Anyway, as to the specifics of that 'moment of genius', and does it work? In this case, it works for me, because we are told all about Ellie's prodigious backstory, but already know that she doesn't let it govern her decisions at all. So, what could often be a moment meant to "astound" the viewer, to portray the protagonist as some sort of superhuman beyond words, all that hackneyed crap..instead serves to bolster the integrity of her character, that she isn't someone who can ever imagine poisoning the science with her own ego. She's probably the smartest person in the room in most instances, but that doesn't even cross her mind - she just wants the science to be pure, for it to reach its full potential.

I thought the whole "can you hear the music" montage was very cliche. Random shots of him walking through a museum, smashing glasses on the ground (for the eccentric genius look), frantically scribbling over a chalkboard, etc. It felt almost like parody to me. I understand that it's hard to show what they were going for without falling back on familiar tropes, but it distracted me with how cheesy it felt. I could imagine him leaning out his dorm window and shouting "eureka!", and it wouldn't feel out of place in that montage.
I personally didn't mind this because the movie needed to convey an idea simply without spending too much time on it. Tropes are helpful that way.

Don't overuse signifiers.  If your character is a genius, it ought to show in the story somehow, assuming it's a relevant detail. 


Don't bow to the lowest denominator in your writing, there's absolutely no need for expository dialogue like "you would obviously know this, being the foremost authority on particle physics". 


Just have it show in the story. Otherwise it's not a relevant detail anyway

I don't have a great example or detailed analysis, I just want to add that I think it's interesting how it can be communicated in one of two ways: 

1. Rhe character is a genius within the mechanics of the film, so the audience understands the effects of their genius. Some examples that come to mind are Hannibal Lecter, Amy Dunne, Lou Bloom, Catherine Tremell, even Mark Zuckerberg. The twists and turns lead directly to the character and it clicks for us as the audience. Maybe this is more "clever" than "genius" but I can see this approach applying to both.

2. The character is a genius in ways that intentionally alienate the audience, often because the subject matter is too complicated to explain within the runtime of the film. Typically that's how scientist films will approach it, including Oppenheimer. The jargon they speak may sound like gibberish to a lot of the audience, and it's not meant to "click." Instead we trust they are a genius by how others react to them, or by seeing their invention when applicable.

I think certain films need these signifiers. If your character is a brilliant detective or something you can show it in the story, sure. But that doesn’t work for something like Amadeus, you really need scenes and dialogue there that are just to reaffirm his genius.

Why can't anyone ask a question about something without trying to deride something else?

Although now, over a quarter-century later, pieces of Good Will Hunting can be seen as cliche, people have to understand that it was a big movie, not an art film. The chalkboard scene is iconic, so, like anything iconic, it's going to be so popular that it appears cliche. I still believe the bar scene when Will schools the "book-smart" student is one of the best "I'm smarter than you" scenes in the history of cinema. Good Will Hunting does a solid job of avoiding the kind of pulp fiction "cheese" that noir detectives carried during the 40s and 50s, but I still don't look back on noir films as cheesy for being what they are. You can pretty much dismiss everything in this manner. Think horror films. Either way, I don't know anyone, young or old, who thinks Good Will Hunting is cheesy, so that strawman of "most people" doesn't ring true to me.

Genius is extremely rare. Hidden genius is even more so. When telling the story of genius, there must be an ah-ha moment for the other characters (and thus, the audience). Ah-ha moments are not subtle, even when they involve other geniuses or near-geniuses. They are flashes of lightning - world-shaking realizations - and need to be expressed as such to the audience, who are generally not near genius. Whether it's the chalkboard in Good Will Hunting, or the match-counting in Rain Man, or rolling through television trivia questions in Quiz Show (or Magnolia, or Diner), there needs to be some hand-holding for the audience. They need a flashing sign or exposition through dialogue that tells them "this person is a genius!"

I think the Diner scene with Kevin Bacon showing how intelligent he is (and thus, how he's wasting his potential) is pretty subtle, but people today may see it as on the nose. Reality Bites would be another example, but everyone talks about how smart Ethan Hawke's character is throughout the film. High intelligence is baked into The Fugitive, but talk about cheesy, right? Or, Apollo 13, where you have dozens of near-geniuses showing off their intelligence throughout the film. But again, super cheesy blockbuster, probably, to "most people." (Yes, I'm giving you shit, but hopefully you understand that I'm doing so in jest). The Matrix? The savior of the world isn't subtle. The Usual Suspects? Ex Machina? Michael Clayton? Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy? The Aviator? The Pianist?
"That pass expires in one week. You're not real FBI."

I thought the "Can You Hear the Music" scene conveyed really well what a great imaginative mind Oppenheimer had. He had such strong and vivid imaginations that he was able to see waves and particles in his mind that were hidden to the human eye. This ability is what made him a great theoretical physicist. 


Later on over the course of the film, especially in the gym speech scene and at the climax of the film, Nolan calls back on this ability of Oppenheimer's to imagine things in a very vivid, almost life-like way when we see how it works less in a scientific and more in an emotional/traumatic way.
That felt cheesy to you? Man I just have a wildly different interpretation of what cheesiness is than most here I guess

What makes someone a genius in a movie is that they do easily what anybody else would find hard.  And, it's the easy with which they do it that shocks those who really know how hard it is.  Capture that shock and amazement, and you'll deliver.  Surprisingly, Oppenheimer (2023) never captured this and that's why we feel like we're being *told* he's a genius without believing it.

The structural problem is that the 'stun' moment has to be smart enough for that first scientist and something that won't make the second expert a complete idiot for not knowing. (like in The Martian when some 'genius' explains sling-shotting to the head of NASA). But at the same time the whole thing needs to be graspable by the audience. The near impossibility of that is probably why we forgive scenes such as the one I mentioned. A simpler way is to have other characters talke about the smart one, they just have to sell themselves as being smart enough that impressing them means the protagonist is super smart.

When you know that "property is theft" isn't a Marx quote, but a Proudhon quote, I think the line serves to show that Oppenheimer doesn't really know what he's talking about but is too proud to admit it — which was why he messed up the quote in the first place. Compare it to the scene where he meets Kitty and she readily admits to not understanding quantum physics.

Additionally, in that moment, the fact that he knew German isn't really about making him look smart in the audience's eyes. We already knew he already spoke German because of the earlier scenes where he went to get his PhD at the University of Göttingen in Germany. It's purely about him trying to make himself look smart in Jean's eyes after he made himself look dumb by messing up the quote.

In my opinion, the scene is a demonstration of his pride more than anything else.

The scene where the critique about knowing language as a shorthand for intelligence is stronger, IMO, is the one where he gives the lecture in Dutch.
I think it's fair to interpret the Marx line as intentional on Nolan's part, but I'm not really convinced. I'll doubt we'll ever know.

Yeah it's definitely just my own personal interpretation of the scene. If it was intentional from Nolan, then cool; if not  (it probably wasn't), then I'll play the "death of the author" card, haha

There are other little mistakes in the movie, too, like the American flags having 50 stars instead of 48 in the scene where he's addressing the cheering crowd after the bomb is dropped on Hiroshima.

But again, I can make up my own interpretation about how the scene is already breaking from reality with Oppenheimer seeing the bright flash of the bomb and the burnt flesh falling off of people's bodies, so  one can interpret the 50-star flag to demonstrate that he realizing the militaristic future of U.S. foreign policy he's just made possible by creating the bomb. Thematically, this connects to his final conversation with Einstein about how he's set off a chain reaction that destroyed the world as they knew it.

At the end of the day, I know that almost certainly isn't what Nolan was going for — I'm not trying to justify his oversights, I'm just having fun with it.
For the flag, you can also interpret it as a (potentially unreliable) memory. I think it was probably a production error (that I didn't notice), but it works that way too.
Funnily enough, the minor quibbles I have with Oppenheimer in this regard are almost the opposite of yours.

Anything you are showing the audience with these scenes should be developing character in some way, not just expository “look how much of a genius this person is”.

Amadeus was great because there were emotions attached to the scenes which are showing his musical genius — e.g., his inability to understand or care how offensive he is to Salieri when he recites and trivialises the entrance march, and the first trigger in a long feud.

>  He does not tell Clarice the unsub's name, location, etc., does not describe his appearance, etc

*actually* he tells Clarice that he's drawn a picture of the "Duomo from the Belvedere." Clarice finds Buffalo Bill/Bob in Belvedere, Ohio.

How can you not love Contact, Gorillas in the Mist, and Trog? Contact and GITM are classics. Trog isn’t cheesy, it’s camp. Joan Crawford treats that role like she’s trying to win an Oscar. She saves the film and gives her character such dignity. Contact and GITM are films where the leads are discounted, they’re underdogs. All three of these films fit what you’re looking for, in addition to being classic films every cinephile must see.

>Often my biggest gripe in these types of films is when scientists explain things to each other that they would all already know. Nolan is bad for this.

Recently rewatched the dark knight trilogy and literally laughed aloud when Maggie Gyllenhaal and the other attorneys were explaining RICO to eachother
[removed]

, I think a fun way to do this would be for the scientific genius to have a litmus test for his friend or foe.. maybe even setting up the rival to take the fall..

" * protagonist *those are the ugliest mammalian eggs! " Normal Norman *mammals don't lay eggs!

* protagonist -  okay note to self - - Beware of the person who doesn't know about  monotremes! 

Or something * along the lines of there are no sharks in rivers!". 

 Point is the more logical a mild scientific error is mentioned, the funnier it is when the scientific truth is spelled out. 


Also having him be finished with grad school and honors is kind of a lazy way to do it but it occurs in real life.. so.

All good points, the only rebuttal in defense I can come up with is that the inspiration for the story is the early days of serial killer research, so the implications that the FBI doesn't fully understand what they're looking for is real to life, just not necessarily real to the time of the mid-90s.

>It did fall back on clichés in regards to knowing language (I read it in the original German).

The movie presents it like genius, but that's just how academia is.

In short, don't cram it into a single line.

Also, don't make it seem independent of hard work. 

That said, I do like the scene in Amadeus where Mozart takes Salieri's music and improves it in real time. It's not unlike the usual genius clichés, but hearing the difference in music is much more appreciable than random scrawls on a chalk board, or a dismissive line of dialogue.

>Recently I thought Oppenheimer did an okay job at this, but I think it was easier in that case because he was a smart man in rooms full of smart people, rather than a singular mind leaving everyone else in the dust.

No, Oppenheimer was the kind of genius that others geniuses said was the smartest man they had ever met. This was something the movie utterly failed to capture. He was the kind of genius that could—and did, apparently on numerous occasions—flip through a new engineering document of fifteen or twenty typed pages in five minutes and instantly understand it well enough to correlate and boil down the relevant points for each individual unit of the project, world authorities in their respective fields, in terms of their own areas of expertise.
Gotham doesn’t exactly hire out of T14.

I'm surprised nobody's brought up Jurassic Park.  Both the novel and the screenplay are masterclasses in characters one-upping each other intellectually, specifically Jeff Goldblum's character Ian Malcolm.

Part of what makes Chrichton's work shine is that he researched topics his characters were knowledgeable about so he could drop tidbits of scientific theory while they're arguing about the ethics of creating life.

I loved that scene. Picasso, TS Elliot, Quantum Physics - modernism through and through. Oppenheimer was a man of his times. Really conveyed the uncharted territories everyone was steering into at that time.
[removed]

I thought it was a bit like the TV show Manhunter - it is set (and in this case made) in a time when psychological profiling (and true crime) wasn't known like it is now.

Silence of the Lambs was pre-internet, and I remember being the only one in my friends and family who'd read books by John Douglas and had a clue about these things.

A quick dip into Google n-grams shows me the word 'unsub' rocketing in usage after that movie, and after Criminal Minds started. These concepts were not broadly known back then.

I know it's a cliche, but I think it's a 'show don't tell' thing.

Instead of having your genius say things that are intelligent, have them do things that are intelligent. This goes all the way back to articles I read as a kid about how to DM a vampire or similar genius in D&D.

The trouble is that you need to understand your audience, and what they may or may not know, and what they would find impressive. Most people know nothing about linguistics, so Louise Banks in Arrival can impress by analysing things in a way that a linguistics professional like me finds easy.

You also have to know cliche, and avoid it, e.g. Oppenheimer reading multiple languages. Perhaps also remember that many people speak multiple languages without being especially intelligent in other ways, and many extremely famous academics don't speak multiple languages.

Some of the things intelligent people do are not sensible. I thought Good Will Hunting worked well because of the scene where he argues in the bar. Not because of the stupid 'apples' joke at the end, but because he's angry. He's frustrated with the Harvard ponytail's conventionality, at the waste of an education, and how this person tries to bully and embarrass his best friend. And he wants to fight him. He's not content to sit there in the corner being intelligent and secure. Will seems the most intelligent where he's mixing intelligence with insecurity and immaturity. Not when he does maths - that's the lame Beautiful Mind/Imitation Game stuff.

Well, A Beautiful Mind is not just a movie about a genius but also about someone who suffered from mental illness. Many movies that tackle such a subject also involve some kind of contemporary medical diagnosis, which can lead to main characters that look like Sheldon from The Big Bang Theory, except that he’s on a dramatic motion picture instead of a TV sitcom. 

From Zuckerberg to Alan Turing in The Imitation Game, the characters always seem to have some kind of unnamed variation of the Asperger Syndrome, before autism became mainstream; they are portrayed as lacking basic perception of social cues. Or they are simply cocky and arrogant like Will in Good Will Hunting. 

I like your example of Amadeus because that movie, way before this contemporary trend, create the image of a genius that didn't fit the social norms of the time, but it didn't look for the easy way out (his inadequacy in other aspects of his public life were portrayed not as an underlying medical condition). Also, that movie was always very grounded on its fictional origins.

As someone currently doing a master’s degree in linguistics I thought that using an apocryphal story (which she acknowledges as untrue) was particularly brilliant as it shows her not only to be a smart person who knows her linguistics shit but she’s also the kind of expert who knows how to explain things to people who aren’t experts in her area (which makes sense, she’s a professor, she explains concepts to students all the time) even if it means the best way to explain it is by using an explanation that’s either hypothetical or otherwise not based in fact

It's extremely hard to do well in movies because that simply doesn't happen in real life. People who are brilliant in a field or practice don't stun others with impressive declarations in dramatic conversations. They just do great stuff that speaks for itself and you can't help but admire them. In conversation they are usually normal people, sometimes interesting clever people, but normal nonetheless. The movies make it cheese because the idea itself is cheesy.

> Zuckerberg totally **pwning** his professor

is this really still a word we're using in 2024 or can we retire it and never bring up how it was ever a thing that people did, just let it fade into the ether
I think you may have failed to pick up on the intended tone there
Or, maybe, you failed to effect a tone

Sure, but that doesn't really enter into the matter here.  A line like that is meant to do some extra lifting; it tells us that he's well read and that he's multilingual, which the man himself *was*.  The fact that the script doesn't support that assertion with thorough research doesn't make its inclusion hackneyed; it just makes the script a little clumsy outside of that facet.
You’re use of the work “effect” here makes me slightly confident in my view

> You’re use of the work “effect” here

your*

word*

"effect" is also a verb, it means "to cause to come into being."
I think you misunderstand. "I've read it in the original language" is the trope to quickly show he's the smart genius surrounded by people less smart.

Good points.

It was my mistake to use "unsub."  I don't recall what word the characters use.  "Perpetrator," "suspect," "scumbag," etc., don't seem to add or lose much--what I mean is a concept about a criminal and how to catch him really doesn't depend upon a term.  You are right: it is the concept that matters; and all agencies which deal with criminals may have their own terms, may even change the terms from time to time.  That doesn't mean they neglect to canvass, etc.

And I too might not have had a clue about such things back then, but surely real and fictional agencies should.  See, I assume, rightly or wrongly, the FBI in the movie know what they're doing.

Good points.

I agree that it is an early entry in a specific genre; but standard police practice, in reality and fiction, predates that by decades. And so do the situations and their consequences. E.g. if an agency wishes to investigate a crime, well, then they need to investigate, and it is common practice to canvass a victim's neighborhood, talk to relatives, etc., as part of that investigation--indeed, it seems inexplicable to me the FBI in the movie hasn't done that and waits as long as it does, and does so only in what seems to me an afterthought.  E.g. if an agency wishes its agents to efficiently canvass a neighborhood, they need to assign more than one agent, even assuming one lone agent will never meet hostility.  I can accept all kinds of fictional things in the story, but this ignoring of common sense seems very odd.  The movie could have been just as entertaining.
